stemMd: The period $T$ of a simple pendulum depends only on its length $L$ and on the acceleration due to gravity $g$. Which of the following expressions has the dimension of a time, and so could be proportional to $T$?
explanationMd:
**What to notice first.** Compare dimensions, not numbers. $L$ is a length (m) and $g$ is an acceleration ($\text{m/s}^2$). To get a time (s) the metres have to cancel, so $L$ must be *divided* by $g$.

**The step that settles it.**

$$\frac{L}{g}\;\to\;\frac{\text{m}}{\text{m/s}^{2}}=\text{s}^{2}, \qquad \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\;\to\;\text{s}.$$

Only the square root of $L/g$ gives seconds.

**How to check it.** Physical sense agrees: a longer pendulum swings more slowly, so $L$ belongs in the numerator, and stronger gravity makes it swing faster, so $g$ belongs in the denominator. The choice with $g/L$ has them the wrong way round, and it turns out to be a frequency.

distractorRationale.c: Inverts the ratio. $g/L$ has dimension $\text{s}^{-2}$, so its root is $\text{s}^{-1}$: a frequency, not a time.
distractorRationale.d: Has dimension $\text{m} \div (\text{m/s}^2)=\text{s}^2$, a time squared. The square root is missing.
distractorRationale.a: Has dimension $\text{m}\cdot\text{m/s}^2=\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2$, the square of a speed. Multiplying $L$ and $g$ never cancels the metres.
distractorRationale.b: Has dimension $\text{m}/\text{s}$: it is a speed. The metres do not cancel when $L$ and $g$ are multiplied.

accessibilityText: The period T of a simple pendulum depends only on its length L and on the acceleration due to gravity g. Which expression has the dimension of a time? The choices are: the product of L and g; the square root of the product of L and g; the square root of the quotient g over L; the quotient L over g, without a root; and the square root of the quotient L over g.

independentSolve.workingNotes: [L/g] = m / (m/s²) = s², so √(L/g) has the dimension of seconds. Lg is m²/s², √(Lg) is m/s, √(g/L) is 1/s, and L/g is s², so none of those is a time. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave7-resolve-held-run1) reached the same answer: [L]/[g] = m / (m/s²) = s², so √(L/g) has the dimension of seconds. L/g has dimension s² and √(g/L) has dimension s^-1. Lg is m²/s² and √(Lg) is m/s, so no other option is a time.]

review.notes: Author's uniqueness check: dimensions: sqrt(g/L) is 1/s, L/g is s^2, Lg is m^2/s^2, sqrt(Lg) is m/s and sqrt(L/g) is s, so exactly one choice has the dimension of a time.
